note.note:
History:
- Presenting complaint: 2 days of lower abdominal (lower tummy/suprapubic) pain, described as central; feels "like with a needle."
- Associated symptoms: mild nausea (no vomiting), feeling hot and sweaty; measured temperature ~37°C one hour prior; slight pink discoloration of urine reported (patient describes "a little bit" of blood); mildly increased urinary frequency; increased thirst.
- Bowel: recent constipation last week now resolved; last bowel movement ~2 hours ago and reported as normal.
- Gynecologic: no vaginal discharge, no intermenstrual bleeding. History of an internal contraceptive implant described ambiguously (“had the implant for one year, now no more”).
- Onset/duration/progression: symptoms began 2 days ago, no previous similar episodes.
- Context: no recent travel. Lives with parents. Drinks alcohol ~1 beer, 4 times/week. Non-smoker.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic illnesses: none reported.
- Surgical/hospitalizations: none significant reported.
- Allergies: Amoxicillin.
- Medications: No regular or over-the-counter medications documented.
- Family history: Mother had breast cancer (treated).

Physical Examination:
- Observed/reported findings: patient reports feeling hot and sweaty; self-measured temperature ~37°C (one measurement).
- Urinary symptoms: slight hematuria reported; no pain on passing urine (no dysuria); slightly increased frequency.
- Pain distribution: central/suprapubic lower abdominal pain; no flank or back pain.
- Other relevant negatives: no vomiting, no vaginal discharge, no intermenstrual bleeding.
- Formal vital signs other than the one self-measured temperature: Not recorded.
- Formal physical examination: Not recorded.

Impression:
- Primary clinical impression: Probable acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) based on suprapubic pain, new hematuria, increased urinary frequency and low-grade systemic symptoms; this was the clinician’s working diagnosis in the consultation.
- Other plausible diagnoses consistent with the history (from DDx, consistent with transcript):
  - Ureteric/renal stone — hematuria plus acute pain could represent a stone, but absence of flank/radiating severe colic makes this less likely.
  - Gynecologic causes (ovarian pathology, PID, or ectopic pregnancy) — can present with lower abdominal pain and nausea; implant/pregnancy status is ambiguous, so gynecologic causes remain possible but are not suggested by vaginal bleeding/discharge in this history.

Management Plan:
- Immediate/recorded actions taken:
  - Offer/prescription of a short course of oral antibiotics: clinician advised a 3-day course, twice daily; prescription to be sent to patient’s allocated pharmacy. (Antibiotic agent/name not documented.)
  - Patient consented to receive and take antibiotics.
- Safety-net/advice given:
  - Start antibiotics as soon as they are obtained.
  - Return/contact immediately if pain worsens, if high fever develops, if back/flank pain develops, or if new symptoms occur.
  - If symptoms are getting worse or not improving, a face-to-face assessment was advised and may be required.
  - If recurrence of the same problem occurs, contact for re-evaluation.
- Medication details: antibiotic duration and frequency documented (3 days, twice daily); antibiotic agent/name and dose/route not documented.

Patient Summary:
- The patient presented with 2 days of central lower abdominal pain, mild nausea, feeling hot/sweaty, and a small amount of visible blood in the urine with slightly increased urinary frequency. The clinician’s working diagnosis was a lower urinary tract infection and a 3-day course of oral antibiotics (twice daily) was offered and will be sent to the patient’s pharmacy. Patient advised to seek urgent review if symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop.

Key Takeaways:
- Begin the prescribed antibiotics (3 days, twice daily) as soon as they are collected from the pharmacy.
- Seek immediate care or contact the service if pain worsens, high fever or back/flank pain develops, or new symptoms occur.
- A face-to-face review may be needed if symptoms do not improve or recur.

Next Steps:
- Patient to collect the antibiotic prescription from their allocated pharmacy and start treatment.
- Contact clinician/service promptly for worsening symptoms or non-improvement; arrange face-to-face assessment if indicated.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: formal vital signs (pulse, BP, respiratory rate, measured temperature by clinician), physical examination findings, urine dip/urinalysis or urine culture results, pregnancy test status/last menstrual period and full sexual history, antibiotic agent/name and dose/route.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none identified (DDx top diagnoses were consistent with the clinician’s working diagnosis and the history); contraceptive implant status is ambiguous in both transcript and DDx (ambiguity noted).
- Transcript quality: moderate — several short inaudible/unclear segments and some fragmented patient responses; implant history and exact phrasing around some symptoms were ambiguous.
